Lecture 3: The Cell Membrane
Objectives
• Describe the structure of the plasma membrane
• Compare passive and active transport
• Explain the role of membrane proteins

Functions of the membrane
• Barrier between the cell and its environment
• Selective permeability
• Cell signalling
• Cell adhesion
• Cell recognition

Fluid Mosaic Model
• Phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins
• Cholesterol regulates membrane fluidity
• Carbohydrates form the glycocalyx used for recognition
• Proteins can move laterally within the bilayer

Transport across the membrane
Passive transport: movement down a concentration gradient without energy
Active transport: movement against the gradient using ATP
Osmosis: diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane
Facilitated diffusion: uses channel or carrier proteins

Types of membrane proteins
• Integral proteins span the bilayer
• Peripheral proteins attach to the surface
• Receptors bind signalling molecules
• Channels allow ions to pass
• Carriers change shape to move solutes

Sodium-potassium pump
1. Three Na+ ions bind inside the cell
2. ATP phosphorylates the pump
3. The pump changes shape and releases Na+ outside
4. Two K+ ions bind outside and are released inside
Result: a steep sodium gradient is maintained across the membrane
notes_en: The plasma membrane separates the cell from its surroundings. It is made mainly of phospholipids and proteins. The membrane controls which substances enter and leave the cell.

Diffusion occurs when particles move from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration. Temperature increases the rate of diffusion because particles move faster. Larger molecules diffuse more slowly than small molecules.

Osmosis is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane. A hypotonic solution causes cells to swell, whereas a hypertonic solution causes cells to shrink. Red blood cells burst in pure water because water enters by osmosis.

Active transport requires energy from ATP. The sodium-potassium pump moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in. This unequal movement creates an electrical gradient across the membrane of about -70 mV in neurons.

dense_en: Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute. It equals stroke volume multiplied by heart rate. Exercise increases cardiac output because both stroke volume and heart rate rise. Preload is the stretch of the ventricular wall before contraction. Afterload is the resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood.

Blood pressure depends on cardiac output and peripheral resistance. Vasoconstriction increases resistance and therefore raises pressure. The baroreceptor reflex detects changes in arterial pressure and adjusts heart rate. A rise in pressure leads to a reduction in heart rate through the vagus nerve.
